With this discovery, Descartes believed he had found the first absolutely secure piece of knowledge: something no doubt and no criticism could overturn, and which could therefore serve as a firm foundation for everything that followed.

His next step was simple. To doubt is to reflect, to think. So the existence of thought is equally certain. I know that thought exists. This is not merely my opinion. It really is the case. It is a truth.
There is hardly anything to argue about here. We clearly cannot doubt the existence of thought, because doubt is already a form of thought.
But Descartes went further than this without realizing that he was doing so. And in doing so he revealed that he had not achieved full self-awareness—that he still lacked “wisdom.”
He did not speak merely about doubt and thought in general. His famous formula was:
“I doubt, or I think, therefore I exist.”
At first sight, this addition seems entirely harmless. After all, it really is I who doubt—Descartes himself.
But in fact, the existence of doubt and thought does not logically require the existence of an “I” that doubts and thinks.
In actual life, of course, thinking is always something a human being does. But logically, things need not be conceived that way. We can imagine thought existing without any particular “I” behind it.

Suppose, for example, that we are trying to solve a very difficult mathematical problem. We can become completely absorbed in the task. We are certainly thinking, but we have no reason to use the word “I.” Our attention is directed at the problem, not at ourselves. We are conscious, but we are not self-conscious.
If we had existed in that state throughout our entire lives, from birth to death, we would never have said “I.” We could never have said, “I think, therefore I exist.”
In other words, we would not exist as a consciously recognized “I”—and therefore, in a sense, would not exist as an I at all, since an I is always aware that it is an I.
We could not ask questions about ourselves. And for that reason, we could not become philosophers or “sages.”
Thought would exist, but there would be no thought about oneself. There would be no “I” toward which thought could turn. There would be consciousness, but not self-consciousness.

Some philosophers—Aristotle, for example, and many others after him—believed that this kind of “thought in general” really does exist. They imagined a kind of “world intellect,” Aristotle’s nous, which thinks without ever saying “I” and without possessing the kind of “personality” we find in a human being who does say it.
This thought thinks itself. If you like, it is even self-conscious. But it thinks itself as thought in general, not as an I that thinks.

The “self” in this kind of self-consciousness is nothing other than consciousness itself. It is not, as it is in a human being, consciousness of a “self” that certainly thinks and is conscious, but is also something more than thought and consciousness—for example, something that acts or desires.

I am not claiming that such a universal intellect or such a “Thought-in-itself” really exists. On the contrary, I will try to show that it does not, and that no thought exists apart from the actual thought of human beings.

But the fact that we can conceive of nonhuman, impersonal Thought is enough to show that, from a logical point of view, the concept of Thought as consciousness is not identical with the concept of the I as self-consciousness.
So if we want to join these two concepts together, we have to explain why.
Descartes does not do that. He simply assumes, without saying so, that Thought is always his thought—“my” thought—and that consciousness is always his own consciousness.
In other words, he not only failed to answer the question of what he was—what this “I” was that thought and doubted. He never even asked the question.
He did not ask why he knows not only that thinking is taking place, but that he is the one thinking.
He did not ask why he is not merely “consciousness,” but also “self-consciousness”; not merely “thought,” but an “I”; or why this I thinks at all.

By failing to ask these questions, Descartes showed that he had not yet reached “wisdom.” Whatever his unquestionable philosophical achievements, his questions and answers did not exhaust all the questions and answers that were possible.
Hegel was the first philosopher to become fully aware of this gap in Descartes. He began his own philosophy precisely by asking where the Cartesian thinking I comes from and why it thinks.
But even in Descartes himself, this gap can already be felt, because it distorts everything that follows in his philosophy.

Because Descartes never asked about the origin of the “I” or about its relation to thought, he treated the existence of a “thinking I” as a bare fact that required no explanation. As a result, he gave a completely wrong answer to the question of what the I actually is.
He went wrong because he began philosophizing too late. He skipped over a whole series of logically necessary preliminary questions.
He took the existence of a “thinking I” as his starting point—that is, as a precondition of philosophy, a fact philosophy itself did not have to explain.
But if philosophy is to have any unexplained starting points at all, they have to be sought much further back.

The thinking I itself can and must become the subject of philosophical questioning. We can and must ask what the I is independently of thought, what thought is independently of the I, and why the I thinks philosophically while its thought is also thought about itself.
Because Descartes failed to see the need for these preliminary questions, he gave a false answer to his first philosophical question: what is this “thinking and doubting I”?
He silently—and therefore unconsciously and unphilosophically—assumed that if a “thinking I” exists, it must exist in the same way that things exist in general, like an atom or a tree.
So once he had established the fact that the thinking I exists as the starting point of his philosophy, he asked his first philosophical question:
“I am a being, or a thing, that thinks.”
At first sight, this seems innocent enough, even persuasive.
It may appear that saying “I think and I exist” is no different from saying “I am a thinking being” or “a thinking thing.”
But the two claims are far from equivalent.
The first is plainly true. The second is plainly mistaken.
From the fact that I think and that I exist, two different conclusions are possible.
We can say, with Descartes, that the I is “a being, a thing, that thinks.”
Or we can say, with Hegel, that the I is “a thought that exists.”
These propositions are not equivalent at all. To say that thought exists is not necessarily to say that thought is a being, or that it exists in the way a thing exists.
There are many ways of existing.

Suppose, for example, that an ashtray really is sitting to the right of an inkwell on my desk. We then have to say that the “ashtray,” the “inkwell,” and the relation “being to the right of” all exist.
But although the ashtray and the inkwell exist in roughly the same way, the relation “being to the right of” clearly exists in a very different way.
Nothing tells us that thought must exist in the same way as things like an inkwell, rather than in the way relations such as “being to the right of” exist—or perhaps in some third way entirely.
So saying that the I is a being or thing that thinks is not at all the same as saying that the I is a thought that exists.
And if the second formula is correct, the first is wrong.
This is not yet the place to explain in detail how I exist or why Descartes is wrong to say that I exist in the way things do. We will return to that later.

For now, I will simply say that identifying the existence of the I with the existence of a thing leads—as it actually did in Descartes—to two doctrines that today we have no reason to accept: spiritualism and deism.
Descartes’s “thinking thing” is, in his own words, nothing other than a soul. And he believes he has proved that this soul is independent of the body, separate from it, and immortal.
We can doubt the existence of our extended physical body. After all, in dreams we sometimes believe our bodies to be completely different from what they really are.
But, Descartes argues, we cannot doubt the existence of our “soul,” because the soul is precisely the thing that thinks. And we cannot doubt the existence of thought.
It follows, in his view, that the existence of the body and the existence of the soul have nothing essential in common.
The defining feature of the body is extension in space. But spatial extension is not necessary for the soul.
The soul could therefore exist, so to speak, outside space. Its existence could be independent of the spatial existence of the body.
It could be everything it is—a thinking being—quite independently of the body.
There would therefore be no reason for it to stop existing when the body disappears.
In other words, the soul would be immortal.
Descartes’s “proof” is neither completely sound nor particularly convincing. But given his starting point, his conclusion is not unreasonable.
If we assume that the thinking I exists in the way a thing exists, then we do have to say that it is a very unusual kind of thing, one deserving a special name: the “soul.”
And once we have made that assumption, it is perfectly consistent to suppose that this “soul” exists independently and eternally.
If the thinking I exists like a thing, then, like every other thing, it must possess definite qualities that belong to it once and for all and do not change.
Here, the sole quality of the thinking thing is its activity of thinking.
But since this activity does not belong to purely material things as such, the thinking I must be an immaterial or “spiritual” thing—that is, precisely what we call a “soul.”
And since this “soul” is a thing with only one essential quality, it cannot be divided into constituent parts. It therefore cannot be destroyed in the way an atom or electricity might be destroyed.
So if we regard the “thinking I” as an immaterial thing, we are led to say that this thing exists eternally. The “soul,” distinct from the body, is immortal.
If there is a law of conservation for material things, then there must also be a law of conservation for the thing called the soul.
But this conclusion leads us into another philosophical error: theism.

If my thinking I is a “soul”—a thing with definite, unchanging qualities—then when I think about this I or this soul, I can think only of the quality it actually contains. In the same way, if I think about iron, I can think only of the qualities of iron, not of some completely different substance.
The sole quality of the “soul” is its activity of thinking. But my thinking is doubting thought—that is, incomplete or imperfect thought.
So when I think about my “soul,” I can think only of an imperfect activity of thought.
Yet I possess the idea of a perfect activity of thought: certain knowledge from which all doubt has disappeared.
This idea cannot have come from thinking about my soul, and still less from thinking about my body, which does not think at all.
So, Descartes concludes, there must exist another, perfect “soul”—namely God. By thinking of this being, I acquire the idea not of my own imperfect knowledge but of perfect knowledge.
On its own, Descartes’s “proof” is not very convincing.
Like all theistic thinkers, he silently assumes that we must first possess the idea of perfection before we can become conscious of imperfection.

And if we also assume—as we should—that being determines consciousness, then if consciousness of perfection must precede consciousness of imperfection, perfect being, “God,” must likewise precede imperfect being.
But this is simply false in practice.
We can become aware that something is imperfect without already possessing an idea of perfection.
To see that a chimneyless hut has a poor heating system, for example, we do not first need to know about houses with electric central heating.
On the contrary, the “perfect” heating system could arise only because someone first became aware that the existing one was inadequate and wanted to improve it by creating something new.
If that is so, Descartes’s “proof” loses all force. As a logical deduction it may be valid, but it begins from a false premise.

Still, as I will only be able to show later, the idea of a thought capable of recognizing an imperfection before any idea of perfection appears is incompatible with the idea of the thinking I as a thing or “substance” endowed with fixed qualities or “attributes” once and for all.

If, when I think about myself, I can recognize my own imperfection, and if by negating that imperfection I can produce the idea of perfection without that idea having existed beforehand, then my I does not exist in the way a thing exists. It exists in some completely different way.
But if we begin by defining the I as a thing, we ultimately arrive at the claim that “God” exists.
And in this sense, Descartes is right.
We should also notice that we have reached the connection already mentioned between theism and the denial that “wisdom” can ever be attained.
Descartes begins from the imperfection of human thought. Human beings will always doubt. They will never reach knowledge from which doubt has disappeared—that is, they will never reach “wisdom.”
If that is true, then there are only two possibilities. Either we doubt everything forever, or we look outside humanity for a guarantee of truth—that is, to God.
And this is exactly what Descartes does.
For him, “God” becomes the one and only “guarantee of truth.”
Strictly speaking, without the idea of “God” I can know only that I exist and that I think—that is, in Descartes’s terms, that I “am a thinking being.”
